title: Topological Frenkel excitons in 2D molecular crystals
authors: Quentin Stein, Sidhartha Nayak, Song Jiang, Jakob Kuhlke, Michelangelo Romeo, Thomas Frederiksen, Fabrice Scheurer, Katharina Kaiser, Tomas Neuman, Guillaume Schull
abstract: Collective molecular excitations govern energy transport in light-harvesting and optoelectronic materials. Theory predicts that excitonic band topology can generate edge-confined states, offering a route to direct energy flow in molecular systems, yet experimental evidence is lacking. Here we use scanning tunnelling microscopy-induced luminescence to image Frenkel excitons in two-dimensional zinc phthalocyanine molecular crystals with nanometer resolution. By varying cluster size, we observe the transition from discrete quantum-confined excitations to collective excitonic bands and directly resolve their real-space wavefunctions. We identify an excitonic state localized at the crystal perimeter and show, through comparison with microscopic theory, that it originates from the momentum-resolved non-trivial topology of the bulk excitonic bands. Our results establish molecular crystals as a platform for engineering topological excitonic states and provide a strategy for controlling energy transport through excitonic band engineering.
summary: This paper investigates energy transport in 2D molecular crystals by linking excitonic band topology to physical observables. Using STML, the authors image excitons and demonstrate that edge-confined states, predicted by non-trivial band topology, can be directly resolved. This establishes molecular crystals as a viable platform for engineering directional energy flow.
main_problem: The study aims to determine if the topological features inherent in the excitonic band structure of molecular crystals can generate robust, edge-confined states that facilitate directional energy transport.
main_result: The researchers successfully imaged and theoretically confirmed the existence of edge-confined excitonic states in 2D molecular crystals, demonstrating that molecular crystals can be engineered for controlled energy flow.
method: The work combines experimental imaging using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy-induced Luminescence (STML) with theoretical modeling based on a Frenkel-exciton Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The physical system is 2D molecular crystals (e.g., zinc phthalocyanine) hosting Frenkel excitons. The model uses a Hamiltonian describing coherent excitonic coupling, with calculations relying on TDDFT to derive transition charge densities.
key_observables: Real-space wavefunctions of excitonic states, spectral features in STML maps, and the identification of edge-localized states linked to non-trivial band topology (Zak phase).
important_parameters: Cluster size ($N 	imes N$), energy eigenvalues ($\Delta E_i$), and the coupling strength derived from dipole-dipole interactions.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes coupling is dominated by dipole-dipole interactions, and that the system can be modeled by restricting the Hamiltonian to the single-excitation subspace.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, STM topographies, and STML spectra, alongside theoretical simulations showing the evolution of excitonic bands from discrete to collective modes, and the spatial mapping of edge states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical problem and experimental technique (STML imaging) to developing the theoretical model (Hamiltonian/TDDFT), and finally demonstrating the key finding: the observation and theoretical confirmation of topologically protected edge states.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges condensed matter theory (band topology) with experimental quantum optics/spectroscopy (STML), providing a tangible platform for studying coherent energy transfer in molecular systems, which is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum light-matter interaction.
